HAKUTO

a ispace inc. Sumitomo Shibakoen Building 10F, 2-7-17, Shiba, Minato-ku, Tokyo, Japan, https://ispace-inc.com/ b The Space Robotics Lab, Tohoku University, Japan http://www.astro.mech.tohoku.ac.jp/e/

Abstract The research focuses on the thermal interface design of the HAKUTO Rover Flight Model (FM) and its evaluation using the final thermal vacuum experiment. Initially, an analytical thermal model was developed, dividing the rover into six distinct radiating surfaces. The surface temperature of the rover was then determined based on its orientation relative to the solar radiative flux, as well as other thermal factors such as lunar radiation, solar albedo, and conduction from the lunar regolith. By considering the impact of these heat sources, suitable mounting locations for the avionics and the angle of the solar panels were determined to optimize the rover's thermal performance and power generation while ensuring the rover's mass remained under 4 kg. After the preliminary thermal analysis, numerical computational simulations were conducted to further elaborate on the thermal response of the final HAKUTO Rover FM design, which was then verified through a thermal balance test in a vacuum environment. Introduction

Recently, there has been an increase in space missions led by private ventures. The Google Lunar X Prize (GLXP) [1] was a competition intended to incentivize the development of low-cost access to the lunar surface with minimal aid from government funds. The competition ended at the end of March 2018 without a winner; however, several companies gained valuable business experiences and successfully developed hardware capabilities in the process. Our team, Team HAKUTO, was selected as one of the five finalists and has successfully completed the development of a lunar micro-rover Flight Model (FM). Team HAKUTO has also developed a unique thermal control system to enable the use of commercial off-theshelf hardware in the extreme thermal environment of the Moon while ensuring the rover remains under 4 kg in mass.

This paper focuses on the thermal design of the HAKUTO Rover, as depicted in Fig. 1, and its evaluation using the final thermal balance experiment in a vacuum chamber. In previous research, thermal vacuum experiments were conducted on a Pre-FM (PFM) prototype to verify the thermal behavior of the proposed design in preparation for FM development [2, 3]. Based on the results of these earlier experiments, we identified necessary improvements to ensure critical components remain within their operational temperature limits for the expected thermal environment.

In this phase, the HAKUTO rover will be attached to the lander spacecraft developed by Team Indus. The rover will be directly mounted onto the lander deck using a Frangibolt, which will be released to deploy the rover onto the Moon. While attached to the lander deck, the rover is partially encapsulated by a box-shaped cover called the Lander interface, which is designed by Team HAKUTO, as depicted in Fig. 2.

Due to the severe mass constraint, we decided against fully enclosing the rover in a box. Instead, we extended four legs from the lander and placed multilayer insulation (MLI) around them to reduce heat exchange between the rover and the lander, as well as between the rover and outer space.  Based on the

interface design agreed upon between Team Indus and Team HAKUTO, the temperature of the lander deck will be maintained above -50°C. Additionally, internal heaters will be used to warm the rover. The heaters and corresponding temperature sensors will be designed by Team HAKUTO but monitored and controlled by Team Indus. Due to the significant limitations in rover size and power, Team HAKUTO thoroughly investigated the layout of the heaters, aiming to minimize heater power while adhering to the design constraints.

*Fig. 2. Conceptual image of the Lander Interface Thrusting Phase During this phase, the main thruster of the lander is activated, creating an exhaust plume that will last for up to 15 minutes. This exhaust plume generates a significant heat load on the rover. To assess the impact on the rover's thermal performance, we conducted thermal simulations meticulously. The results of these simulations have provided confirmation that the rover's temperature will remain within its designated thermal range throughout the duration of thrust operations. Deployment Phase Until the rover is deployed, the temperature of the lander deck will be actively controlled, ensuring that the rover remains within its designated operating temperature range. However, once the rover is detached from the lander and deployed onto the Moon, there is a possibility that it may end up in a shadow zone, with the lander blocking the sunlight. In such a scenario, the rover will be unable to receive any energy from the sun for power generation.  During this phase, it becomes crucial to assess the duration for which the rover might remain in shadow and determine how soon it will need to leave these shadowed regions. This assessment is vital to ensure the rover's power is maintained and its operations will not be compromised. Surface Operation Phase*

Radiometer Experiment (Diviner) [4]. A lunar period lasts approximately 28 Earth days, encompassing both lunar day and night, spanning about two Earth weeks. As the rover relies solely on solar panels for power generation [3], the mission is designed to operate within a single lunar day.

The timing of the mission start is crucial due to the extreme temperature conditions during lunar sunrise, where lunar temperatures can drop to -200°C. To mitigate the risk of failures caused by these low temperatures, we have determined that the mission should commence no earlier than 50 Earth hours after lunar sunrise, allowing the surface temperature to reach at least -20°C in the target region at 28° latitude. During lunar noon, the rover will experience the maximum heat from the sun and the lunar surface [3]. According to the profile of the lunar surface temperature, we have made the decision to establish a mission period during which the rover's temperature should be maintained within its designated operating temperature range. This mission period is defined as starting 50 hours after the local dawn and lasting until 50 hours before the local sunset.

Based on the Diviner data, Hurley et al. [5] have successfully developed a mathematical model to predict lunar surface temperatures. The tuning factor (n) is incorporated to match the temperature profile in sunlit conditions. *Fig. 4. External and internal heat flow on the lunar surface. 2.2 Design Concept We implemented isolation between the body panels of the rover to simplify the thermal design process. By reducing the number of thermal interactions to consider, we can more easily assess and validate trade-offs. Initially, we divided the rover into six distinct thermal zones: top-rear-front, right, left, bottom, as well*

as the wheels on the right and left side, as depicted in Fig. 5. To achieve isolation between these zones, we incorporated two thermal isolation measures. Firstly, we utilized a high thermal resistance material to minimize thermal conduction between the zones. Secondly, we employed multi-layer insulation (MLI) to reduce radiation. This approach allows us to treat each node independently during the preliminary design phase, as they do not have thermal interaction with one another. Assuming a steady-state condition, the temperature of each node was calculated separately, as depicted in Fig. 6. This isolation concept provides a solid starting point and enables faster design iterations in the preliminary design phase, allowing for efficient thermal analysis and optimization. In our design, we strategically placed all of the electronics on the top, rear, and front surfaces of the rover, as depicted in Fig. 7, considering the fact that these surfaces have smaller view factors to the lunar surface.  The top surface, in particular, does not have a direct view factor to the lunar surface. This makes it relatively easier to design its heat balance by considering only the solar radiation (Qs), heat generated from on-board electronics (Qe), and radiation emitted back to outer space (Qsp). To further optimize the thermal design, front, rear, and side surfaces were oriented upward to avoid the lunar radiation factors.  On the other hand, bottom surface is inevitably oriented towards the lunar surface. As a result, it is thermally coupled with the lunar surface's temperature, which can vary significantly throughout the mission period. Due to this coupling, the bottom surface is considered the least favorable place to position thermal sensitive items on the rover.

To ensure an agile and lean design cycle, we implemented an iterative design flow consisting of two phases: an analytic simulation phase for quick assessments and a numerical simulation phase for detailed analysis.

In the analytic simulation phase, we determined steady-state temperatures for each node by utilizing a spreadsheet-based parametric analytic model based on the equations discussed earlier in this paper (Eq 3-9). Using this information, we conducted a trade-off analysis involving the size of the top radiator, the angles of the side panels, and the angles of the rear and front surfaces to identify the optimal mechanical design for the rover.

In the subsequent numerical simulation phase, we performed finite element model simulations based on the rover concept developed during the analytic phase. This phase enabled us to calculate more precise heat exchanges that were intentionally not considered in the preliminary phase.

2.5 Component Layout based on Classification In addition to the basic thermal design concepts discussed in previous sections of this paper, the requirement for a compact rover prompted us to further optimize the layout of the electronics board on the top radiator. We divided the electronics components into two groups: thermal-sensitive components and thermallytolerant components. The first group includes the battery and the radiation sensor, while the remaining electronics belong to the second group. These components were organized into temperature groupings known as the cold zone, where the temperature is controlled between -5°C and +40°C, and the hot zone, where the temperature ranges from -30°C to +65°C, as depicted in Fig. 10. Consequently, since we only needed to size the radiator to maintain the temperature within the specified limit for each zone, we were able to significantly reduce the size of the radiator. A picture of electronics layout of the FM rover 2.6 Indented Radiator In the HAKUTO mission, during the final design phase, the lunar latitude of the new landing site was changed to a lower value than initially planned, and the deployment timing of the new landing profile was advanced compared to the original plan set by the prime*

payload customer. As a result, the lunar surface temperature exhibited greater variations according to the new mission profile, with colder temperatures in the lunar morning and hotter temperatures at lunar noon. This necessitated an extension of the thermal design to accommodate a wider temperature range, while still maintaining the integrity of the main structure design to minimize impacts on the mechanical design and manufacturing process. To address this challenge, we introduced a unique design approach known as the indented radiator. The indented radiator consists of two components: an angled surface painted black to enhance heat absorption and a flat surface covered with Ag-Teflon, as depicted in Fig.12. When the sun's inclination is low and the lunar surface temperature is also low, the system effectively absorbs heat through the angled surface. Conversely, when the sun's inclination angle is high and the lunar surface temperature is high, the system receives less sunlight. This design mitigates temperature variations experienced by the rover throughout the mission duration. However, it is important to note that this design will increase the maximum temperature experienced by the rover due to the black coating applied to the angled part, in contrast to its original state of being covered with Ag-Teflon and being flat (i.e., this design will reduce the temperature variations but increases the hottest temperature experienced by the rover). Finally, we carefully designed the depth and angle of the indented structure to minimize temperature variations over time and ensure that the maximum temperature remains within the nominal operating range of the rover.

3. Key Simulation Results 3.1 Cruise Phase

We developed a simulation model of the cruise phase and identified the minimal heater power and margin necessary for the rover to survive in this phase. 3.2 Thrusting Phase

We conducted transient analysis of the rover’s temperature during thrust operations and confirmed that none of the components would exceed their storage temperature limits. 3.3 Deployment Phase

After conducting a transient analysis of the rover’s temperature during the deployment phase we found that the rover will have to move out of the shadow region within an hour of its deployment. This operational constraint has been accommodated in the operational plan. 3.4 Surface Operation Phase

4.2 Thermal Balance Test Simulating Cruise Phase

To simulate the cruise thermal environment, we utilized a thermal vacuum chamber. The rover was securely mounted on a thermally controlled base plate, which was maintained at a temperature of -50°C to mimic the lowest temperature experienced on the lander deck during the cruise phase. Additionally, we exposed the rover to the cryogenic chamber wall, which was set to a temperature of -170°C, as depicted in Fig.14. More detailed thermal profile is presented in Fig. 15. Figure 16 shows the actual photography of the cruse environment test.

By comparing the measured temperatures with the simulation model, we verified that the temperature deviation of the mission-critical electronics components was within a margin of less than 5°C. This indicates that the thermal design successfully maintained the required temperature levels for these crucial components during the simulated cruise phase.

## 5. Discussion

Through simulation, we have confirmed that the design of the rover adheres to its specified operating and storage temperature ranges with a 10°C margin (except for the battery, which has a 5°C margin) throughout all mission phases. However, to meet the design requirements, the rover necessitates a heater and orientation control during the lunar morning.

Furthermore, a thermal balance test was conducted, which demonstrated that the actual thermal behavior of the rover aligns with the simulation model within a deviation of 5°C. This confirms the consistency between the simulated thermal performance and the actual performance of the manufactured rover.

Lastly, the final mass of the rover, including the interface to the lander deck, is less than 4 kg.

aunque Antonio Neumane hubiera optado por hacerlo, así como Francisco Rosa — tras la muerte del primero— la evidencia sugiere que ninguno de los dos contrató a un profesor con el propósito específico de enseñar a futuros intérpretes. Más bien, si hubiera surgido una situación en la que un estudiante quisiera estudiar oboe, al parecer esa responsabilidad habría sido asumida por los flautistas Rafael Jiménez o Pietro Traversari. De esta manera, Ecuador aparentemente siguió un tipo de enfoque “generalista” que se estaba utilizando durante este período no solo en los varios países de Centroamérica, sino también en América del Sur. Por ejemplo, un año después de que Enrico Marconi llegara a Ecuador en 1870, el gobierno colombiano envió una delegación a Italia donde contrató al director de banda, Juan De Sanctis, quien fue descrito como un “virtuoso” de casi todos los vientos, así como de violín y el piano.3

En el período comprendido entre 1870 y 1876, la ausencia de un profesor de oboe también nos puede informar sobre el estado de la música instrumental y la apreciación de la misma durante aquella época, tanto en el Ecuador como en muchos de los países latinoamericanos. Como sugiere el musicólogo mexicano Oscar Mayer-Serra, ya que el público “estaba acostumbrado a considerar los conciertos [de solistas instrumentistas] sólo como una exhibición acrobática,”4 la gente culta esperaba más bien un tipo de actuación musical que incluyera una cierta cantidad de “espectáculo.”5 Así que, en vez de un solo de oboe, los artistas que llegaron al Ecuador durante las últimas décadas del siglo XIX generalmente eran violinistas o pianistas.

En 1900, el gobierno ecuatoriano intervino nuevamente en el área musical reestableciendo el Conservatorio Nacional, y, como antes, poniendo a cargo de la

administración a profesores extranjeros. Durante los once años de administración, el plantel no contó con un profesor especializado en oboe. No obstante, el cinco de noviembre de 1903, la institución presentó un concierto de estudiantes que incluyó un cuarteto de vientos madera que interpretó una obra de Luigi Hugues (1836- 1913).6 Aunque el nombre de cada instructor sigue (en paréntesis) al de cada uno de los estudiantes intérpretes, dado que el nombre del instructor se indica como “P. Traversari,” no queda del todo claro a qué Traversari se hace referencia.7 No obstante,

es importante señalar que el oboísta miembro del cuarteto fue José María Ortí, quien posteriormente fue nombrado instructor de oboe del plantel. Tres años después, el 25 de julio de 1906, el Conservatorio presentó un concierto de clausura, en el cual un grupo de instrumentistas de viento interpretó el mismo cuarteto de Hugue. Dentro de la lista de intérpretes no figura el nombre de Ortí y aparece como miembro de este grupo el oboísta Manuel Villamarín.8

Al mirar hacia la administración del Conservatorio durante la década de los 1870, se podría argumentar que el período regido por Marconi/Brescia (1900-1911) representa un grado tangible de mejora. Sin embargo, al compararlo con instituciones similares de la región, queda claro que Ecuador se había rezagado. Por ejemplo, en 1894, el uruguayo (formado por un oboísta italiano), José Garayalde, llegó a Santiago

de Chile como oboísta principal del teatro municipal de esa ciudad. Cuatro años después, fue nombrado miembro del cuerpo docente del conservatorio nacional de ese país. Aún más revelador es lo que ocurrió en Colombia, donde en 1886, el nombre del flautista y oboísta Jenaro D’Alemán aparece en una lista de profesores y empleados de la academia nacional de música de dicho país. De hecho, él había llegado a Colombia en 1873.

La historia del oboe en el Ecuador durante el resto del siglo XX continuó de una manera esporádica e inconsistente. Poco después del despido de los profesores italianos en 1911, parecía que se iba a establecer algo de continuidad cuando el cargo de profesor de oboe pasó de maestro a estudiante: Julio César Villamar (n. 1894), discípulo de Miguel Jaramillo (1885-1950), ocupó dicha plaza en el Conservatorio hasta por lo menos 1950. Sin embargo, no hay ninguna información sobre quienes fueron sus estudiantes. Seis años más tarde, llegó a Quito el oboísta guatemalteco Manuel Gómez Samayoa (1916-1990). Este célebre oboísta fue uno de los diez intérpretes extranjeros reclutados para formar parte de la Orquesta Sinfónica Nacional del Ecuador (OSNE) en su primer concierto.9 Como profesor de oboe en el Conservatorio Nacional, formó a Edgar Pineda (1943-2025).

Después de que Gómez abandonara Ecuador posiblemente en 1960, el Conservatorio parece no haber contado con un profesor de oboe sino hasta 1964, cuando llegó al país el oboísta francés Lucien Ladet (1926-2000). Uno de sus estudiantes más exitosos es Daniel Fellig (n. 1961), quien en 1986 triunfó en un concurso de jóvenes solistas. Luego, se perfeccionó en la Universidad Estatal de Luisiana. No obstante, ya que actualmente el Conservatorio no cuenta con un profesor de oboe, se podría decir que esta situación ha vuelto a la normalidad. En otras palabras, a lo largo de la presencia institucional del oboe en Quito, tristemente, ha existido un descuido, cuando más bien, ha habido múltiples oportunidades como para seguir el ejemplo de casi todos los países vecinos.
